headline: Execution Rocks goes dark-hours only as bass slide into a nighttime pattern
subhead: Warm shallow water has the bass feeding after sundown while fluke and bluefish carry the daylight shift from Throgs Neck to Matinecock.
body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop on City Island Avenue asked me Tuesday why his son's been getting skunked at Execution Rocks fishing the same 10 a.m. slot that used to load the cooler back in May. Told him straight — that window closed a month ago and it's not reopening till the water cools off in September. The western basin's running warm, Kings Point reading 72 and change, and warm shallow water pushes keeper bass onto a low-light clock. If you're fishing Exec Rocks or the Stepping Stones in broad daylight right now, you're fishing for bluefish and short bass, not the 30-inch class that's actually around.

I've watched this pattern play out for three decades on this stretch and it doesn't change — it just shows up earlier or later depending on the year. Right now the money bite at Execution Rocks is the last two hours of light into full dark, working the ebb as it starts pulling water off the rockpile toward the Sound. Eels on a fish-finder rig, or a bunker chunk fished on the bottom in 25 to 35 feet on the northeast face, has been the ticket. Guys anchoring up tight to the rock and soaking bait through the change of tide are doing better than the trollers running bucktails through there at noon. Stepping Stones is the same story — that light marks a highway for a reason, but it's a nighttime highway in July. Work the flood as it builds against the light structure, live bunker or a big swimbait worked slow along bottom, and give it till after 9 p.m. before you write off a spot.

We're sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, and that's going to soften the current everywhere from the Throgs Neck Bridge down through Matinecock Point. Neap tides aren't a death sentence — they actually open up some of the structure fishing that gets blown out by a hard moving tide. If you've been getting your teeth kicked in trying to hold bottom at Hart Island on a big tide, this is your window. Slower water means you can work jigs and bucktails more methodically over the rockpiles without getting swept off the structure every ten minutes.

Daytime hours belong to fluke and bluefish right now, and both are worth your gas money. Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing going in this whole zone — channel edges off Throgs Neck, the drop-off along Hart Island, and the deeper water off Matinecock Point have all been giving up fish in the 3 to 5 pound range, with the occasional 6-pounder mixed in. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide, are outfishing bait rigs for me the last two weeks. Fish the tail end of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping — that's when the fluke set up on the edges waiting for stuff to get swept off the flats.

Bluefish are the daylight show. Bunker schools have been stacking up off Matinecock same as they do every June and July, and the blues have found them. I've had mornings off Matinecock where the water just erupts — bunker skyrocketing, blues underneath tearing through the pod. Nothing fancy needed there — a bucktail or a diamond jig thrown into the commotion, or a topwater popper if you want the visual. That bunker-and-blues pattern tends to hold as long as the weather stays calm and settled, and right now it has been, so I'd expect it to keep rolling through the basin toward Execution Rocks and down past the Throgs Neck over the next week unless we get a blow that scatters the bait.

Porgies are around but I'll be honest with you — the grade's down from what Montauk guys are posting. We flagged that a week ago and it's held up. You're getting decent numbers of scup in Hempstead Harbor and off Manhasset Bay on sandworms and squid strips over the mussel beds, but they're mostly hand-sized, not the slabs the eastern end guys are icing down. Fine for a fish fry, not a wall hanger.

Weakfish have been showing sporadically in the shallower back bays — Manhasset Bay and up in Little Neck Bay on the last of the incoming, usually mixed in with the short fluke. Nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around, but if you're already out there working the flats, drop a bucktail with a strip of squid down and see what happens.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for the pattern to flip. The neap tide through the 21st and into the weekend is going to keep current soft at the rockpiles, which favors patient bottom fishing over covering water. If you want bass, commit to the dark hours at Execution Rocks or the Stones and fish it right through the tide change rather than one spot for twenty minutes. If you want numbers in the box, the fluke grounds off Hart Island and Throgs Neck are the safer daytime bet, and the Matinecock bunker pods should keep the blues honest as long as this weather holds.
